P6a: What impressed me most was their idea of authority, mandar obedeciendo, which means leading by obeying. The representatives carry out what the assemblies decide, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.
P6b: What impressed me most was their way of handling leadership, this idea of mandar obedeciendo: leading by obeying. Basically, the representatives carry out what the assembly decided, and they're accountable to the people who gave them the mandate.
P7f: The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because their autonomy goes beyond how they vote. They've set up their own education and health care, and their own justice. They run their own collective production and political training. They've also worked out their own ways of teaching outsiders, all while coordinating beyond a single village.
P9f: After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. Their new arrangement moved authority toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community. Those local governments can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as depending on the communities instead of sitting above them.
P10a: Most institutions add layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas looked back at theirs and pushed authority down. Instead of putting out a leadership book and a certification program, they changed the system they were actually living in.
P10b: The pattern in most institutions is that they pile up layers and offices as they age. The Zapatistas reviewed theirs and moved authority down. They didn't write a book on leadership and start a certification program, they just changed the system they were actually living in.
P11f: This is also where I have to rein in my enthusiasm. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. They've fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades. A new ecovillage can't copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.
P12a: The Zapatistas themselves have warned people not to import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. It's okay to copy how they learn, though. They build something and ask questions, and when something isn't working the way it's supposed to, they change the structure.
P12b: The Zapatistas themselves have warned people not to import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. What you can take from them is the way they learn: they build, they ask, they find out where the practice fails, and they change the structure.
P13a: The Zapatistas also don't prove out my whole economic path, where a community starts with unpriced internal necessities, moves to a common purse, and eventually stops using outside money. Their communities do pool their work to keep schools and clinics running, and to support their autonomous government and their resistance. But they also sell products and trade, and they get support from outside. What they show is that a community can take major necessities and public functions off the market and govern them together. Outside help can make a community more capable. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, if the specialist, the donor or the organization stays indispensable.
P13b: They're also not proof of my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money altogether. P15a: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where people's lives turn into a performance of community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.
P15b: An escuelita can fail by turning into a visitor business. The residents end up spending their lives performing community for outsiders who pay, and the number of guests becomes the measure of success instead of the number of daughter communities. Making people feel transformed for a week isn't the point. The point is teaching enough of the social and material system that some of them can go build it somewhere else.
P16a: In my research I also looked into what came out of the Escuelita. There are alumni networks, and people took practices home and organized later. But I couldn't find a clean chain from one Escuelita student to a new communal institution, with evidence of how its members and their kids actually did over time. And Zapatista influence was spreading internationally before the Escuelita, so a later resemblance doesn't prove it came from there. So I'm borrowing a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate it. I'm not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.
